messages.subject: Factors in sqldf files created by read.csv.sql
messages.subject_clean: Factors in sqldf files created by read.csv.sql
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to figure out how to create an SQLite database containing  roughly 30 gig of data from the Census's Current Population Survey (CPS) in a form where I can get the data back out without having to do complicated joins on with multi-gig files that create memory problems. I know that this is not what sqldf was created for, but it does seem to be set up to understand R data types. This is crucial for my application, as most of the columns -- over 300 of them -- are factors.

If I am understanding the documentation correctly, columns in sqldf objects normally take their data class and factor levels from the data frames they are read from, and pass that information back to R with any data extracted from the sqldf object. My question is, if I read the data in using read.csv.sql, to avoid the R memory bottleneck, is there an alternate way to inform the sqldf file what the data types and factor levels are?

Finally, if I am reading multiple files into a single sqldf object, will I have difficulty if some columns have the same names and some do not? And specifically, can I assign data types to just the new columns, and expect that the shared columns will take their data type from the previous assignment, or would that lead to the kind of the conflicts that disable column class as described in FAQ section #1.

Any help or pointers would be much appreciated.

Sincerely, Andrew

On Tuesday, October 1, 2013 3:27:36 PM UTC-4, Andrew Hoerner wrote:
> I am trying to figure out how to create an SQLite database containing  roughly 30 gig of data from the Census's Current Population Survey (CPS) in a form where I can get the data back out without having to do complicated joins on with multi-gig files that create memory problems. I know that this is not what sqldf was created for, but it does seem to be set up to understand R data types. This is crucial for my application, as most of the columns -- over 300 of them -- are factors.
>
> If I am understanding the documentation correctly, columns in sqldf objects normally take their data class and factor levels from the data frames they are read from, and pass that information back to R with any data extracted from the sqldf object. My question is, if I read the data in using read.csv.sql, to avoid the R memory bottleneck, is there an alternate way to inform the sqldf file what the data types and factor levels are?
>
> Finally, if I am reading multiple files into a single sqldf object, will I have difficulty if some columns have the same names and some do not? And specifically, can I assign data types to just the new columns, and expect that the shared columns will take their data type from the previous assignment, or would that lead to the kind of the conflicts that disable column class as described in FAQ section #1

read.csv.sql is just a thin wrapper around sqldf.  It sets up the arguments appropriately so what applies to sqldf mostly applies to read.csv.sql too.  The sqldf method= argument determines how classes are assigned to output columns and  is described in ?sqldf .  The default is method = "auto" but you can use other valid values described there and you can also use your own function as described there as well.  Also you could just employ the method = "raw" argument (which uses the classes as they come from RSQLite) and then change the classes of the output yourself.  For example:

    to.factor <- function(DF) {
        is.char <- sapply(DF, is.character)
        replace(DF, is.char, lapply(DF[is.char], factor))
    }

    # 1
    DF <- read.csv.sql("myfile.csv", method = "raw")
    DF <- to.factor(DF)

    # 2 - or equivalently
    DF <- read.csv.sql("myfile.csv", method = to.factor)

I am not clear on the last question but if you are rbind'ing data frames normally they should have the same names.  There is rbind.fill in the plyr package which can handle cetain situations where the names are not the same.  If you are combining them using sql union then the tables must have the same number of columns and same types.

Your test.bat script works for me so it may be that #Rscript.bat is not on your path as you suggest.  Try this from the Windows cmd line:

     where #Rscript.bat

If it responds that it can't find it then #Rscript.bat is not on your path.  Note that you do not have to put all of the batchfiles on your path -- you only need to put #Rscript.bat on your path.  The files in batchfiles, including #Rscript.bat, are each self contained and none depends on any other file.

If you issue this command from the Windows cmd line:

    path

it will give you your path so just put #Rscript.bat in one of those directories.

sequences_subset <- sqldf("SELECT * FROM sequences WHERE time > 2013-09-13")
sequences_subset

sequences_subset <- sqldf("SELECT * FROM sequences WHERE time > 2013-09-13")
sequences_subset

I've been playing around with method = "Date", but don't know how to apply it to a single column. I know I should RTFM, which I have done, but find it very difficult to decipher.

Any help would be much appreciated.

Best,
Aron

Using the dput output to recreate sequences, as str shows the column named "time" is of class POSIXct:

> str(sequences)
'data.frame':   10 obs. of  3 variables:
 $ id   : int  1545 1545 1545 1544 1544 1543 1542 1541 1541 1541
 $ event: Factor w/ 14 levels "assigned","closed",..: 3 2 3 2 3 8 8 3 3 3
 $ time : POSIXct, format: "2013-09-14 01:23:55" "2013-09-14 01:23:57" "2013-09-13 18:58:00" "2013-09-14 01:36:57" ..

SQLite has no date/time type so such columns are stored in SQLite as the number of seconds since 1907-01-01 00:00:00 GMT.  We can use the SQLite strftime function to convert such a number to text and then do the comparison using text strings:

> sqldf("select * from sequences
+ where strftime('%Y-%m-%d', time, 'unixepoch', 'localtime') > '2013-09-13' ")

    id     event                time
1 1545 discussed 2013-09-14 01:23:55
2 1545    closed 2013-09-14 01:23:57

3 1544    closed 2013-09-14 01:36:57
4 1544 discussed 2013-09-14 01:36:55

An alternative would be to use the H2 database backend to sqldf for this because the H2 database does support a date/time type.  In that case it would just be this:

> library(RH2)
> library(sqldf)
> sqldf("select * from sequences where time > '2013-09-13 23:59:59' ")

    id     event                time
1 1545 discussed 2013-09-14 01:23:55
2 1545    closed 2013-09-14 01:23:57

3 1544    closed 2013-09-14 01:36:57
4 1544 discussed 2013-09-14 01:36:55

In the above as RH2 is loaded, sqldf will notice that and use RH2 instead of SQLite.  Note that RH2 is a java database and java must be installed for the above to work Java has an automated installer and is very easy to install.  Only need the java runtime is needed.  The java development environment is not needed.

messages.body_plain:
1. There could be a writeback argument that wrote back every table after every SQL statement:

    sqldf("alter table mytable add column mycolumn number", writeback = TRUE)

This does have the downsides of
- possibly clobbering existing data frames making it less safe and
- it could result in overhead of copying back tables that had not changed and
- since R data frames don't have keys if sqldf read the data frame into sqlite, added a key and wrote it back the key would be lost which suggsts we may be getting into an area of increasing complexlity

2. Another possibility is to automatically prefix certain table names with main. although it has these downsides:
- it changes the SQL statement whereas currently that is never the case so you can be absolutely sure what is being passed to the driver
- it is database system speciifc.  For example, PostgreSQL does not use main.

The current system seems conceptually purer but I will think about it a bit more and may experiment with a writeback argument.
